title: DRC Ebola Outbreak Becomes Deadliest in Country's History With 2,325 Deaths
excerpt: The three-month-old outbreak caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain has killed 2,325 people with 4,945 confirmed cases, surpassing the 2018-2020 toll and becoming the second-deadliest Ebola epidemic on record globally.
body:
• The DRC's current Ebola outbreak has killed 2,325 people with 4,945 confirmed cases, surpassing the 2018-2020 outbreak to become the country's deadliest ever.
  • The Bundibugyo strain driving the outbreak has no approved vaccines or treatments, and the case fatality ratio has climbed to 46 percent.
  • Armed conflict in eastern DRC, community resistance, and a $400 million funding gap are hampering the response effort.
  • Uganda successfully contained its linked outbreak, limiting it to 20 cases and 2 deaths before discharging its last patient in July.

A Grim New Record

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has become the deadliest in the country's history, with 2,325 deaths and 4,945 confirmed cases as of August 16, according to government data reported by CNN. The toll surpasses the 2,299 deaths recorded during the 2018-2020 outbreak that was previously the DRC's worst.

https://x.com/XHNews/status/2089165797935763701

Globally, the outbreak is now the second-deadliest on record, trailing only the 2014-2016 West African epidemic that killed more than 11,300 people across Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. The pace has been alarming: it took that outbreak nearly five months to reach 1,000 deaths, while the DRC's current crisis hit 2,000 in less than three months.

The outbreak, the DRC's 17th, was formally declared on May 15 after cases emerged in Ituri province in the country's restive northeast.

No Vaccine, Rising Fatality

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola virus, which has triggered only three outbreaks in recorded history and has no approved vaccines or specific treatments. Existing Ebola vaccines target the Zaire strain and offer no protection against Bundibugyo.

The case fatality ratio has climbed from about 20 percent in early June to 46 percent, meaning nearly one in every two confirmed cases is now fatal. Experts say this does not indicate a more lethal virus but rather persistent failures in surveillance and case detection.

"We're still seeing many cases detected very late, when treatment is less likely to succeed, with many identified only after they die in the community."

— Thomas Parisch, Médecins Sans Frontières

Ituri province accounts for 88 percent of all confirmed cases and 82.6 percent of deaths. Among healthcare workers, 151 have been infected and 44 have died — a fatality rate of 29 percent.

Conflict and Resistance Hamper Response

Active armed conflict in eastern DRC is compounding the health emergency. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus reported in July that an Ebola treatment centre in Bunia was attacked, and more than 80 percent of new infections were being detected outside known contact lists — a sign of widespread undetected transmission.

About two-thirds of deaths occur in communities among people who never reach a health facility. Community resistance to health teams, fueled by distrust and misinformation, continues to obstruct contact tracing and safe burials.

The crisis has had cascading effects on broader healthcare. The United Nations Population Fund reported that maternal deaths in outbreak regions have doubled, with an average of six women dying per week from childbirth complications as pregnant women avoid medical facilities for fear of Ebola exposure.

Global Response Falls Short

WHO has warned that the outbreak is "continuing to outpace the response" despite substantial scale-up: treatment capacity has grown to more than 800 beds, laboratory capacity has expanded from one facility to 16, and over 21,000 community health workers are being trained.

But funding remains the critical bottleneck. WHO and Africa CDC's joint response plan faces a gap of more than $400 million. UNICEF said only 25 percent of the funding needed for its Ebola response was currently available.

"We know how to stop this epidemic. The challenge is not the lack of solutions, but the lack of funding to deploy them at the scale needed."

— Gilles Fagninou, UNICEF Regional Director

The United Nations Development Programme estimated the outbreak could cost Africa up to $3.6 billion and 328,000 jobs in a worst-case scenario where the disease spreads to neighbouring countries including Rwanda and Angola.

Uganda Contains Its Outbreak

In a rare bright spot, neighbouring Uganda successfully contained its linked outbreak. The country's last confirmed patient was discharged in July after testing negative twice, starting the 42-day countdown before the outbreak can be officially declared over. Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases and two deaths, with 15 infections linked to importation from the DRC.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies has warned that the DRC epidemic may not have peaked and could last a year or longer. With no vaccine in sight and conflict raging across eastern Congo, the trajectory remains deeply uncertain.
nri_angle: The outbreak poses global health security risks, with WHO and UN agencies calling for international funding support to prevent further cross-border spread.
